content: Prosthetic and orthotic devices should not only meet the technical criteria but also be comfortable, functional, aesthetically acceptable, and aligned with the user’s needs and expectations. From an economic perspective, a high-quality prosthesis or orthosis is one that is durable and cost-effective. These criteria, along with others, define the concept of appropriate technology. The concept of quality should extend beyond technical work to encompass prosthetics and orthotics services in a broader sense. High-quality services are user-centered, physically and financially accessible, and free from other barriers. Users should feel they have been treated with respect, experience minimal waiting times, require fewer visits, and have their safety ensured. The working processes should be appropriate, the technical quality of the products should be high, and continuity of services should be guaranteed. This includes follow-up care, maintenance, product renewal, and referrals to other services. These aspects of service delivery influence the trust beneficiaries place in the services, their willingness to seek assistance, their likelihood of returning to the center if needed, and their motivation to recommend the services to others. This, in turn, affects the overall outcomes and impact of the services. Quality management in prosthetics and orthotics services involves all actions taken by service providers to measure, monitor, and improve the quality of products and services, ensuring that all requirements for adequate service delivery are met. This includes defining quality indicators, which measure the quality achieved for each feature, and quality standards, which outline the requirements to be met. Quality standards should be based on the best available evidence and aligned with national or international standards, such as those set by ISO, WHO, or ISPO. These standards must be realistic and reflect the context in which the services are provided. Benchmarks may be established to measure gradual improvements in quality over time. Quality can be assessed and monitored through structural and clinical testing (for technical quality), user satisfaction surveys (to measure service quality), analysis of service data and statistics, or occasional quality controls by external experts. Monitoring quality can reveal problems and identify actions required for improvement. These actions may include revising manufacturing processes to enhance product durability or modifying appointment procedures to reduce waiting times for users. Any system affecting the quality of products and services, including management, administration, financial procedures, material procurement, stock management, and professional training, may need to be adjusted. Quality assurance is not a one-time task but a continuous process performed in a cycle. Once problems are identified and corrective actions are taken, quality should be re-measured to verify improvements. Occasionally, quality indicators may need to be redefined to ensure all necessary aspects of quality are accurately captured. Similarly, standards may be gradually adjusted as quality improves. The quality management cycle involves identifying problems, measuring quality, monitoring, taking action to improve quality, preparing plans, and defining quality indicators and standards. Quality management in prosthetics and orthotics should be an integral part of service provision. Responsibility for this work should be assigned to clinical or technical staff in smaller units or to a quality management team with representatives from various service sections. User and caregiver opinions should be carefully solicited to measure service quality, and feedback should be systematically collected from representative users through methods such as questionnaires or focus group discussions. Service user representatives and organizations for disabled individuals can play a crucial role in facilitating this work.
